title: Fuel Costs Hurt United Airlines' Profit

paragraphs: United Airlines is a large airline in the United States. On Tuesday, October 20, it warned investors that its profit at the end of the year will be weaker than they expected. The reason is the high price of fuel. For any airline, fuel is a crucial cost, and its price is still high.

First, the good news. From July to September, United earned $17.9 billion in revenue. That was 17% more than in the same months of 2025, and it was a record for the company. United also carried a record 49.5 million customers in those three months.

People clearly still want to travel. Revenue from premium seats rose 17%. Revenue from loyalty, the program that gives points to frequent fliers, also rose 17%. Even basic economy, the cheapest kind of ticket, grew 16%. Cargo, the goods that United carries in its planes for other businesses, rose 23%. These numbers demonstrate that demand is strong. People in the best seats, frequent fliers and travelers on a small budget are all spending more.

Nevertheless, fuel put a heavy burden on the airline. United spent 62% more on fuel than a year earlier. That is $1.8 billion extra in just three months. When fuel costs rise this fast, the profit margin on each flight gets smaller. In other words, the airline keeps less money from every dollar it earns. A thin margin is hard to sustain for a long time.

The bigger strain is still ahead. For October to December, United expects earnings of between 50 cents and $1.50 for each share. That is less than Wall Street expected. United says it will pay about 45 cents more for the same amount of fuel than Wall Street had assumed. According to the company, that difference alone is worth about $1 for each share. So the company says the problem is fuel, not a lack of customers.

United's news highlights a problem for the whole airline business. Airlines rely on fuel for every flight, and they cannot simply fly without it. They also rely on customers who keep buying tickets. That second part looks good for now. United says its revenue from October to December will grow more than 20% from a year earlier and set another record.

So the news is good and bad at the same time. Customers are paying more than ever, and loyalty and cargo are growing. But fuel is the burden that United cannot control. The airline warned that the strain from fuel will make its profit weaker at the end of the year. The crucial question is whether it can sustain strong profits while fuel stays expensive, and whether other airlines can do the same.
